paragraphs.text: FEDERAL COURT
Court File No.: IMM-6821-25 (FICTIONAL)
BETWEEN:
DMITRI OSTROVSKY-MBEKI
Applicant
- and -
THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION
Respondent
APPLICANT’S MEMORANDUM OF ARGUMENT
(Application for Leave and for Judicial Review, Rule 10 of the Federal Courts Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection Rules, SOR/93-22)
PART I – OVERVIEW

1.	The Applicant, Mr. Dmitri Ostrovsky-Mbeki, seeks leave and judicial review of the decision of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) Officer dated July 22, 2025 rejecting his application for protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA).

2.	The Applicant is a citizen of a country he fears returning to because of his political activities as a union organizer. His refugee claim was refused in 2019 on credibility grounds and an appeal to the Refugee Appeal Division was dismissed. He applied for a PRRA in 2025 with new evidence of a warrant issued against him in 2023 and a letter from a former colleague who was detained.
PART II – FACTS

3.	The PRRA application included a copy of an arrest warrant, an affidavit from the Applicant explaining how it came into his hands, and two news reports about the colleague’s detention. The Officer found the warrant to be of “little probative value” because it could not be authenticated and rejected the colleague’s letter as “self-serving.” The Officer declined to hold an oral hearing.
PART III – ISSUES

4.	The Applicant raises these issues: (a) Did the Officer unreasonably reject the new evidence under paragraph 113(a) of IRPA? (b) Did the Officer breach procedural fairness by making credibility findings without a hearing, contrary to paragraph 113(b) of IRPA and section 167 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 (IRPR)?
PART IV – ARGUMENT
A. Standard of review

5.	The merits of a PRRA decision are reviewed on the reasonableness standard: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at paras 10 and 23. A reasonable decision must be internally coherent and justified in relation to the facts and the law (Vavilov at paras 85 and 99). Breaches of procedural fairness are reviewed on a standard that is akin to correctness; the question is whether the process was fair in all the circumstances: Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] 2 SCR 817 at paras 21–28.
B. The Officer unreasonably rejected the new evidence

6.	A PRRA officer may not consider evidence that was reasonably available before the refugee decision, unless it is new in the senses set out in paragraph 113(a). The factors are credibility, relevance, newness and materiality: Raza v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385 at para 13. The warrant post-dates the RAD decision. It is therefore new.

7.	The Officer’s concern was authentication. But the Officer did not say what further proof was needed, and did not engage with the Applicant’s affidavit. As the Supreme Court stated in Vavilov at para 128, reasons must be responsive to the submissions. The Officer’s one-sentence dismissal of the colleague’s letter as “self-serving” also is not an adequate basis: see the facts above at para 3 about the corroborating news reports.
C. The Officer made a credibility finding without a hearing

8.	Section 113(b) of IRPA provides that a hearing may be held if the Minister is of the opinion that it is required, on the prescribed factors in section 167 of the IRPR: (a) whether there is evidence that raises a serious issue of the applicant’s credibility and is related to the factors set out in sections 96 and 97; (b) whether the evidence is central to the decision; and (c) whether the evidence, if accepted, would justify allowing the application.

9.	In Singh v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FCA 96 at paras 49–54, the Federal Court of Appeal held that where an officer rejects evidence on credibility grounds in all but name, the officer’s decision is subject to the section 167 factors, even if the officer uses the language of sufficiency. Ibid. The Officer here said the warrant “could not be authenticated”, which is, in substance, a finding that the Applicant is not credible. All three of the section 167 factors are met.
D. The risk assessment was incomplete

10.	The test under section 96 requires a “serious possibility” of persecution: Adjei v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1989] 2 FC 680 (CA) at 683. Under section 97 the test is whether the Applicant is more likely than not to face a risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment: Li v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FCA 1 at paras 33–34. The Officer did not assess either test separately and treated the question as one of credibility. See Canada (Attorney General) v Ward, [1993] 2 SCR 689 on the elements of the definition of a Convention refugee.
PART V – ORDER SOUGHT

11.	The Applicant asks that leave be granted, that the PRRA decision be set aside and that the matter be remitted to a different officer for redetermination, with an oral hearing if the Minister’s delegate considers it necessary. In the alternative, the Applicant asks for a stay of removal pending determination of this application.
